items.title: A Student-Centered Model for Ethically Evaluating AI Integration in Learning Support Services and Beyond
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change

items.title: AI for Everyone: Designing an Introductory AI Course Across Disciplines
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes virtually every field, universities face a growing imperative to ensure AI literacy is not reserved for computer science majors alone. This panel presents the collaborative design of an introductory AI course built for undergraduate general education — one that serves students across disciplines, regardless of technical background. Two co-designers will share the story of building the course from complementary angles. The first presenter will address the technical foundation of the curriculum: how core AI concepts such as machine learning, data, and algorithms were translated into accessible, hands-on learning experiences for non-specialist students. The second presenter will explore the philosophical framework woven throughout the course — examining questions of ethics, agency, bias, and what it means to be human in an age of intelligent machines. The panelists will discuss how technical and philosophical threads were intentionally integrated rather than siloed, creating a course where students not only understand how AI works, but are equipped to think critically about why it matters. Attendees will come away with practical insights on curriculum structure, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and strategies for making AI education inclusive for students from diverse academic and experiential backgrounds. This session is designed for faculty, instructional designers, and administrators interested in developing or expanding AI literacy offerings at their institutions.

items.title: AI Tutors, Worksheets, and Task Design: Matching AI Tools to Learning Structure
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students as a learning resource in STEM courses. However, classroom observations and survey data suggest that unstructured AI use may correlate with reduced student achievement. Two concerns are especially relevant: AI systems can produce incorrect responses in tasks requiring precise validation, and students may use AI in ways that reduce active engagement with course material. This session presents two instructional approaches designed to address these limitations: structured AI-generated worksheets and in-chat AI tutors. AI worksheets generate controlled sets of practice problems within instructor-defined course constraints. In-chat tutors provide interactive practice through problem generation, Socratic questioning, and feedback-driven guidance. The usefulness of each approach depends on the structure of the learning task. Drawing from iterative development and testing primarily in introductory chemistry, we examine four types of tasks: (1) conceptual and explanatory, (2) structured tasks with low ambiguity, (3) multi-step quantitative tasks, and (4) highly deterministic symbolic or structural tasks. Examples from chemical nomenclature, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, Lewis structures, laboratory writing, and mathematical validation illustrate where different AI approaches worked reliably—and where they did not. Participants will receive ready-to-use prompts for both AI worksheet systems and in-chat tutors, along with implementation strategies and observed limitations. The session concludes with a practical framework for selecting AI tools based on the structure of the learning task rather than disciplinary content alone.

items.title: AI-Aware Student Recommendations for GenAI in Higher Ed
items.abstract: What do well-informed students say about the use and integration of AI in their college educations? In Spring and Summer 2026 semesters, students in three sections of ENG 102 at UNR wrote AI-aware white papers with policy recommendations for the integration of genAI into higher education. To develop white paper policies, students read a variety of scholarly, public, and popular sources that show a variety of perspectives on Generative AI and LLMs, including the environmental and cognitive impacts. Then they considered the values and concerns of their audiences—peers, professors, and/or university administrators—to propose “sensible, well-informed, and well-reasoned” policies. This session will discuss their recommendations, insights, and the somewhat surprising classroom experience of teaching sustained, critical enquiry about Generative AI.

items.title: Building Bots That Teach Thinking: Using Custom AI Chatbots to Enhance Critical Thinking and Decision-Making
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly common in education, but its effect on student learning depends largely on how it is used. This interactive session will introduce practical strategies for creating custom AI chatbots that encourage students to think through problems rather than simply ask for answers. Participants will explore ways to design bots that ask learners to explain their reasoning, consider alternative perspectives, identify assumptions, and revise their thinking before receiving feedback. Examples from healthcare education and other disciplines will show how these tools can support guided inquiry, reflective questioning, clinical reasoning, and decision-making. Participants will review and revise sample chatbot instructions, then begin developing a bot for a course or learning activity of their choice. The session will also cover practical considerations such as choosing reliable source materials, setting appropriate boundaries, protecting student privacy, testing the bot before use, and refining instructions based on its responses. Participants will leave with sample prompts, practical design principles, and a plan for using a custom chatbot in their own educational setting. The goal is to help educators use AI in ways that preserve productive struggle, provide a safe environment for practice, and strengthen students’ ability to explain and defend their decisions.

items.title: Crafting Resilient AI policies for Education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into academic spaces requires a shift from passive restriction to resilient, active pedagogical frameworks. This virtual panel explores actionable strategies to protect academic integrity, promote deep critical thinking, and manage AI use, particularly in foundational courses. Panelists will discuss the implementation of high-engagement classroom interventions. The will offer frameworks for transparent student disclosure practices. Attendees will leave with practical templates for syllabus policies, assignment rubrics, and disclosure benchmarks designed to foster a culture of transparency and process-oriented learning in an AI-permeated landscape.

items.title: Designing Custom Chatbots for Classroom Use: Practical Examples, Benefits, and Current Limitations
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have made it increasingly possible for individual educators to design and implement their own custom chatbots without advanced programming skills (Abe & Kaneshige, 2025). This workshop introduces practical examples of custom chatbots developed for educational purposes and discusses both their affordances and limitations for classroom use. We would like to share a chatbot creation experience, which we spent one hour building, with a 30-minute presentation. For each chatbot, we will explain its intended purpose, target users, basic specifications, and expected classroom applications. We will also describe the development process, including how the presenters designed the chatbot instructions, refined prompts, and adjusted the chatbot behavior through iterative testing. After introducing these three examples, the workshop will discuss the potential benefits of custom chatbots. In particular, we will show how they can help users access relevant information more efficiently, provide more focused guidance than general-purpose AI tools, and support educators who want to create AI-assisted learning environments tailored to specific instructional goals. The workshop will critically examine current limitations. Even after repeated tuning, custom chatbots may still produce inaccurate, incomplete, or contextually inappropriate responses. Therefore, developers and educators remain responsible for checking the accuracy of the content and deciding whether the chatbot output is appropriate for learners. By combining demonstration, reflection, and critical discussion, this workshop aims to help participants understand how custom chatbots can be used responsibly and realistically in educational settings.

items.title: Designing with Intent: A Comparative Analysis of Custom AI Chatbots as UDL-Aligned Tools for Multidisciplinary Instruction
items.abstract: The growing presence of AI in higher education has prompted instructors to move beyond passive adoption, to deliberate theory-grounded design. This session presents two custom AI chatbots (DisneyBot and Rico) developed within a teacher preparation course as the technology-enhanced component of a multidisciplinary instructional unit. DisneyBot is built on the ChatGPT platform to guide learners through an exploration of Disney parks, and Rico, is built on the Gemini platform as an interactive guide to information about Puerto Rico by scaffolding learning across four subject-specific lesson modules – Social Studies, ELA/ENL, Science, and Spanish. Both chatbots were developed to support differentiated and interactive learning for 4th and 5th grade students through a virtual field trip framework, with the broader goal of connecting classroom content to authentic real-world experiences. The design of each chatbot was grounded in UDL principles (CAST, 2018). Rather than serving as static information repositories, the chatbots were intentionally designed to function as interactive instructional mediators which use prompting inquiry, guiding subject-specific exploration, and offering differentiated entry points for learners with varying needs and language backgrounds (Vygotsky, 1978). The differences between the two platforms, in terms of interface architecture, customization depth, persona design, and interaction affordances, form the basis of a comparative analysis that will anchor the session. Participants will interact directly with both chatbots, examine the instructional design decisions behind them, and leave with a working framework for developing purpose-built AI chatbots that can be tailored to their own teaching contexts and disciplines.

items.title: EMERGING HEPATOPROTECTIVE THERAPIES FOR LIVER DISEASE: CURRENT PROGRESS AND FUTURE DIRECTION
items.abstract: Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

items.title: Enhancing the Accessibility of Instructional Content in Higher Education Through AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, it presents new opportunities to enhance the accessibility of instructional materials. This session examines how Microsoft Copilot, Adobe AI, and built-in Windows 11 features such as live auto-captions can support more accessible content creation and remediation across Microsoft 365 applications and PDF workflows. Focusing on commonly used instructional formats including Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and PDFs shared through learning management systems, this presentation highlights how AI tools can assist in identifying and addressing accessibility barriers. Examples will illustrate how Copilot can support content development, organization, and alternative text generation, while Adobe AI tools streamline improvements to PDF structure, tagging, and usability. Windows 11 auto-captioning features will also be discussed as a way to enhance access to audio and video content. The session explores practical approaches for integrating AI-supported accessibility strategies into existing teaching and course design workflows. Attention is given to aligning these approaches with accessibility standards and inclusive teaching practices while maintaining efficiency for instructors, instructional designers, technologists, and teaching assistants. Attendees will gain insight into key strategies, considerations, and potential applications of AI to create more inclusive, accessible instructional materials.

items.title: Guardrails in the Classroom: Possible responses by Higher Education to the current moment
items.abstract: This closing discussion seeks to draw out the larger questions about higher education's role in this current moment of AI technology debates, based on the takeaways and ideas for next steps by presenters at this summit. This year's summit submissions centered on practical, classroom-level questions such as: how do we structure assignments so AI supports rather than replaces thinking, how do we teach students to catch AI's confident errors, and how do we build institutional policy on articulated values rather than reactive rules? The presentations on these questions arrive at a moment of a much larger and more unsettled conversation. This year has seen prominent AI researchers — including some from the companies building these systems — publicly disagree about whether increasingly autonomous AI agents pose risks at the scale of catastrophic societal disruption. We cannot resolve that debate here, and none of this summit's sessions were designed to, but this is the backdrop against which conversations about AI in knowledge creation now takes place. This closing discussion asks about the role of higher education when the tools adopted are described, even by some building them, as not fully understood and possibly dangerous — and needs to be taught about AI now in higher education. items.title: IT Meets Academia: Giving Students the Tech Tools to Write the AI Rules
items.abstract: An AI administrator walks into an Honors English seminar. The assignment: prepare undergraduates to help write the course AI policy. This UNLV case study follows an unusual collaboration between a professor of postcolonial literature and the administrator of the university’s ChatGPT and Claude environments. The administrator also wrote UNLV’s draft institutional AI framework and experiences classroom AI rules as a PhD student. The session asks what becomes possible when the person who sees the systems behind the interface joins faculty and students in the policy conversation. Before students could write the rules, they needed enough technical literacy to understand what they were governing: model limitations, learning tradeoffs, differences between consumer and institutional accounts, data practices, authorship, transparency, and personal boundaries. The presenters will trace how that foundation prepared students to participate in course policy development. Dr. Beth Rosenberg will share why she invited IT into an English seminar, how students responded, and how the policy took shape. Attendees will leave with an adaptable model for combining IT knowledge, faculty expertise, and student agency to create AI expectations grounded in both technology and learning.

items.title: Resisting AI with Paper: Possibilities, Concerns and Protest
items.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

items.title: Simulating the Clinical Encounter: Using AI Personas for Risk-Free Mental Health Assessment Practice
items.abstract: Mental health assessment requires students to navigate complex conversations involving depression, anxiety, mania, psychosis, suicide risk, and other sensitive clinical situations. Yet opportunities to repeatedly practice these conversations in a safe, low-stakes environment can be limited. This session demonstrates an innovative approach to using generative artificial intelligence as an interactive patient simulation tool in nursing education. Rather than using AI simply to generate written assignments or answer questions, students interact with AI-generated patient personas designed to exhibit specific psychiatric symptoms and communication patterns. Through spoken or conversational interactions, students practice conducting mental health assessments, asking therapeutic follow-up questions, recognizing clinical cues, and adapting their communication as an encounter unfolds. During this interactive session, participants will see a live demonstration of an AI-simulated mental health encounter and experience how thoughtfully constructed prompts can transform generative AI into a repeatable practice environment. Practical examples will illustrate how faculty can design patient personas representing conditions such as depression, mania, anxiety, and psychosis while incorporating appropriate educational guardrails. The session will also address the role of faculty oversight, limitations of AI-generated responses, and the importance of positioning AI simulation as preparation for, rather than a replacement for, authentic human clinical experiences. Participants will leave with a practical framework for creating AI patient personas and ideas for incorporating low-risk, repeatable conversational practice into their own nursing courses.

items.title: Three Things about AI: Something you already know; Something you may not know but is important; Something you probably don't know, but knowing will be very helpful to you
items.abstract: Presentation, “Three things about AI” as presented to the League of Oregon Cities, Salem, OR, 16 October 2026, by Pam Dixon, Founder and Executive Director, World Privacy Forum. The presentation is a three-part discussion. Part I begins with an area most policy experts and lawmakers are familiar with: the need for high-quality AI risk assessment. HUDERIA is the Council of Europe’s richly detailed methodology for the risk and impact assessment of AI systems from the perspective of human rights, democracy and the rule of law (approved by the Committee of Ministers, 26 February 2025), attached to a binding treaty; COBRA is its Context-Based Risk Analysis model (approved 25 February 2026). Both are non-legally binding, in-depth guidance resources that parties to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI may use or adapt in whole or in part. They are tools that anyone can use. The World Privacy Forum converted the lengthy, paper-based COBRA assessment into an interactive web tool, with all COBRA text verbatim to the edition of record. Applied to an AI system, the tool does not create legal obligations; correctly done, the assessment can reveal risks and / or obligations that may already be present. Part II is a discussion of what people might not know about, which is what the protocol layer of AI systems is, and what constitutes it. Without understanding this part of the AI ecosystem, it is difficult to craft effective legislation or policy regarding AI systems. The deck locates the protocol layer in the ecosystem stack, the one layer every interaction crosses, and spells out some key protocols that now constitute it: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is shown vertically, moving from an agent to its tools and data. The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) and Agent Network Protocol (ANP) are shown horizontally, as the movement is from agent to agent, with their versions and stewardship as of 2 October 2026. Part III is a discussion of what people most likely don’t know about, and that is clustering, the step in which a system sorts people into groups by similarity. Clustering is the core operation of AI as it acts on people, and it is among the most significant knowledge and governance blind spots for technical and non-technical practitioners alike: governance experts and attorneys miss it at the technical level, technical experts miss the law, and between them lies the governance gap neither side covers. The blind spot is that a group is manufactured by the clustering analysis — AI does not describe a community, it constructs a group and acts on it; membership is inferred, no one opts in. This is where normative ideals that are shared by a community, a city, a state, the Pacific Northwest, or a nation become directive. For example, Oregon has law for the person (the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act) and law for named protected groups (Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 659A). But it has no law for the groups the pure data math creates. Because the groups that machine learning forms for itself — as distinct from the classes it is handed — are subject to a mathematics that is both unbounded and unstable, protecting all of them, none of them, or some of them is a trilemma in which none of the answers suffice. Unbounded, because no limit can be set on the groupings that a similarity space admits; unstable, because no canonical grouping exists (this goes back to Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem) and the groups move as the system retrains. One of the solutions available is technical protocol layer governance, but with provenance of authority baked into the overarching ecosystem: four fields — which authority, what mandate, contestable how, revisable when — carried with every category assertion and every grant of authority an AI agent acts on, and gated at assignment, at composition, and at re-advertisement. Governing the protocol layer is necessary but not sufficient by itself. The protocol layer only carries the rules; it is the normative layer that can provide direction (what groups to protect, for example) and teeth (ability to enforce decisions). Neither acting at the protocol layer nor developing good norms suffices alone. It is the deliberative, normative decisions that legislatures make that can then be carried technically through the protocol layer. While norms and laws are governance that sits outside of the protocol layer, they have an impact on how the protocols act, and which ones get written in, and what they accomplish. Lineage: the clustering and deployed-capacity slides were first presented at the Council of Europe plenary “Hack the Hate, Renew Democracy,” Strasbourg, France, June 2026, where the two-bodies-of-law slide used Convention 108+ and hate-speech law in place of the Oregon statutes. The Provenance of Authority concept using some of this deck was presented at AI for Good, Geneva, Switzerland, to Study Group 17 of the ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector on 9 July 2026. The ideas in the slides are further articulated in Theme #5, “Provenance of Authority for Agentic AI,” of the ITU Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI (FG-TIDA), 14 August 2026. The concept of the governance trilemma is treated at length in a Springer book chapter by the author, accepted and peer reviewed, that awaits publication in 2027. The deck closes with three references for advanced reading — Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem for clustering, the Taylor, Floridi and van der Sloot volume on group privacy, and the Shokri, Stronati, Song and Shmatikov paper on membership inference attacks — followed by a sources slide (all addresses accessed 2 October 2026) and a lexicon of every abbreviation used.

items.title: Trust but Verify: Testing a Framework for AI Interrogation in Nursing Education
items.abstract: Generative AI produces fluent, confident output that is sometimes fabricated. Nursing students increasingly submit work built on sources that do not exist, or that exist and do not support the claims drawn from them. This session reports two semesters of classroom observation testing whether prompt design can address that problem. The hypothesis was that structuring student prompts to require the AI to validate its own sources would improve detection of hallucinated citations. It did not. Across two sections, students who used the structured format caught fabricated citations at the same rate as students given an open prompt. Structure did change something: structured students were substantially more likely to notice that something was wrong, but no more likely than the open-prompt group to finish the check. The session presents both rounds, including the confound identified in the first and removed in the second, and the limits of the observation, among them students who did not use the assigned structure. It also reports an unplanned finding: the AI tool used to review the submissions produced the same category of error it was reviewing for, misattributing a real paper to a fabricated author across multiple students before the error was caught on human review. Attendees will leave with a way to check sources that starts cheap and gets expensive, a clearer view of why you cannot ask the model to check its own work, and a specific account of where student checking breaks down.

items.title: Agentic Synthesis of Open-Source Biomedical Repositories and Clinical Literature into Interactive Diagnostic & Medical Learning Tools for Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
items.abstract: Frontline community health workers (CHWs) and rural clinics in low-resource settings—particularly across underserved municipalities in South Asia and rural regions of the United States—face a severe clinical knowledge bottleneck. While peer-reviewed biomedical literature, genomic variant databases, and open-source clinical calculators expand exponentially, these resources remain fragmented across unstructured texts and incompatible software repositories that require high-bandwidth connectivity and specialized bioinformatics literacy. This research protocol introduces **`gwf-clinical-synthesis`**, a non-commercial, computational dry-lab framework developed at GoWithFund Inc. Leveraging long-context multi-agent reasoning in **Google Antigravity** powered by **Gemini 4 Argon** (1M-token unified context window) and the **Google DeepMind (GDM) Science Skills** ecosystem, our pipeline orchestrates parallel literature retrieval across PubMed/NCBI Entrez, OpenAlex, ClinVar, and ChEMBL, fuses fragmented open-source clinical simulation repositories into lightweight offline-capable web applications, and executes automated multi-agent citation-verification loops to eliminate large language model (LLM) hallucinations. Concurrently, we integrate geospatial and socio-economic vulnerability indicators via AlphaEarth Foundations to model optimal healthcare resource allocation across high-burden districts. All resulting datasets, verification benchmarks, and interactive medical learning modules are released open-source under Apache 2.0 and CC BY 4.0 licenses.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Agents and Consumer Behavior: A Bibliometric Analysis of an Emerging Research Field
items.abstract: Recent dynamic advances in AI technologies have brought about profound transformations in the marketing paradigm and in consumer behavior and interactions. At the heart of this transformation, the relationship between AI agents and consumer behavior stands out as a timely area calling for in-depth investigation in the literature. This study constitutes a bibliometric analysis undertaken to reveal the intellectual accumulation of knowledge in this conceptual domain and to examine the evolution of the literature systematically. To this end, 438 articles indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 2020 and 2026 were subjected to a comprehensive examination. The research first conducted a performance analysis to resolve the quantitative structure of the field, mapping annual publication distributions, the most prolific authors, the most highly cited studies, leading countries, and institutional collaborations. It then carried out citation, co-citation, and co-occurence analyses using science mapping techniques in order to structure the intellectual framework of the field. The findings show that the AI agent literature emerging in the context of consumer behavior is following a growth trend that is gaining momentum in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Thematically, the literature was found to concentrate on the transparency and interpretability of AI algorithms, the implications of these algorithms for consumer attitudes and behavior, the strengthening of human-AI interaction through anthropomorphic design elements, the dark side encompassing ethics, privacy, and trust, and sectoral reflections in the service industry.

items.title: Beyond Digital Adab: A Conceptual Model of Ta’dib-Oriented Character Pedagogy in Islamic Education
items.abstract: Digital Islamic learning presents challenges involving unverified religious claims, artificial intelligence outputs, privacy concerns, and unequal access. This study aims to reconstruct the philosophy of ta’dib as a conceptual foundation for character education in digitally mediated Islamic learning. It employs a qualitative conceptual approach through purposive document analysis and an integrative synthesis of literature on educational philosophy and digital ethics. The findings propose the Ta’dib-Oriented Digital Character Pedagogy (TDCP) model, comprising five dimensions: epistemic integrity, dignified interaction, responsible digital agency, equitable participation, and reflective self-discipline. These dimensions are implemented through a cycle of inquiry, deliberation, action, and reflection to support formative assessment and protect learner privacy. The model offers a pedagogical framework for developing ethical reasoning without equating observable behavior with piety. Expert validation and empirical testing are needed to assess its applicability in educational settings.

items.title: CABARAN GURU BAHASA MELAYU DALAM MENGAPLIKASIKAN TEKNOLOGI DIGITAL SEMASA PROSES PENGAJARAN DAN PEMBELAJARAN: SATU TINJAUAN LITERATUR BERSISTEMATIK (The Challenges Faced by Malay Language Teachers in Applying Digital Technology During the Teaching and Learning Process: A Systematic Literature Review)
items.abstract: ABSTRAK: Pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran (PdP) Bahasa Melayu semakin diberi perhatian selaras dengan perkembangan pendidikan abad ke-21 dan transformasi pendidikan digital negara. Walau bagaimanapun, guru Bahasa Melayu masih berhadapan dengan pelbagai cabaran dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital secara berkesan semasa PdP. Oleh itu, kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengenal pasti jenis teknologi digital yang digunakan oleh guru Bahasa Melayu, meneliti cabaran yang dihadapi dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital serta menghuraikan cara guru mengatasi cabaran tersebut. Kajian ini menggunakan pendekatan Sorotan Literatur Sistematik (Systematic Literature Review, SLR) berpandukan garis panduan PRISMA. Sebanyak 15 artikel jurnal yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2021 hingga 2025 dan memenuhi kriteria inklusi telah dipilih serta dianalisis secara tematik. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa platform pembelajaran digital, aplikasi kolaboratif dan produktiviti digital, multimedia digital, aplikasi gamifikasi serta media sosial dan komunikasi digital merupakan teknologi yang dominan digunakan dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu. Cabaran utama yang dihadapi guru ialah kesukaran mengintegrasikan teknologi digital dalam PdP, kekurangan pengetahuan dan kemahiran digital, kekangan internet dan kemudahan teknologi, kekangan teknikal dan penyediaan bahan digital, penglibatan serta kesediaan murid, dan cabaran penggunaan teknologi baharu seperti kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence-AI). Bagi mengatasi cabaran tersebut, guru mengaplikasikan pelbagai strategi seperti memperkukuh latihan dan kolaborasi profesional, meningkatkan kompetensi digital, melaksanakan PdP yang interaktif dan berpusatkan murid, menambah baik akses teknologi serta memanfaatkan gamifikasi dan multimedia digital. Kajian ini memberikan implikasi bahawa pembangunan kompetensi digital guru dan penyediaan infrastruktur teknologi yang mencukupi perlu diperkukuh bagi memastikan keberkesanan pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu.Kata kunci: Teknologi Digital, Guru Bahasa Melayu, Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran, Sorotan Literatur Sistematik, Pendidikan DigitalABSTRACT: The integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning has gained increasing attention in line with the advancement of 21st-century education and the national digital education transformation agenda. Nevertheless, Malay language teachers continue to face various challenges in effectively implementing digital technology during the teaching and learning process. Therefore, this study aims to identify the types of digital technologies used by Malay language teachers, examine the challenges encountered in integrating digital technology, and explore the strategies employed to overcome these challenges. This study adopted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the PRISMA framework. A total of 15 journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 that met the inclusion criteria were selected and analysed thematically. The findings revealed that digital learning platforms, collaborative and productivity applications, digital multimedia, gamification applications, and social media and digital communication tools were among the most frequently used technologies in Malay language teaching and learning. The major challenges identified include difficulties in integrating digital technology into teaching practices, limited digital knowledge and skills among teachers, inadequate internet access and technological facilities, technical issues and digital material preparation, student engagement and readiness, as well as challenges associated with emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). To address these challenges, teachers employed various strategies, including strengthening professional training and collaboration, enhancing digital competencies, implementing interactive and student-centred teaching approaches, improving access to technological resources, and utilising gamification and digital multimedia. The study implies that continuous development of teachers’ digital competencies and adequate technological infrastructure are essential to ensure the effective integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning.Keywords: Digital Technology, Malay Language Teachers, Teaching and Learning, Systematic LiteratureReview, Digital Education

items.title: Challenges and the Repositioning of Islamic Religious Education Teachers in the Era of Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Perspective from Islamic Epistemology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is reshaping how students access, produce, verify, and communicate information, raising questions about source authority, adab, values, and character formation in Islamic Religious Education (IRE). This study examines the challenges facing IRE teachers and proposes a repositioning of their roles from an Islamic epistemological perspective. A qualitative library research approach was employed, drawing on literature on Islamic education and epistemology, teacher ethics, UNESCO guidance on AI in education, and recent studies on AI and IRE. Sources were examined through content and conceptual analysis. The findings position AI as a supporting instrument subject to human epistemic oversight and identify teachers’ roles as knowledge curators, information validators, digital ethics mentors, learning designers, and exemplars of adab. AI outputs should be evaluated within the relationship among revelation, reason, experience, scholarly tradition, and technology. The study proposes the IRE teacher as an epistemic gatekeeper responsible for safeguarding information quality, guiding verification, and aligning technology use with Islamic educational aims. To support implementation, it introduces the Verifikasi model, comprising source verification, ethical use, reflection, integration of religious evidence, process orientation, human initiative, and accountability. The study contributes a conceptual basis and an implementation model for repositioning IRE teachers, emphasizing that AI integration should strengthen literacy, critical reasoning, and adab while preserving human responsibility in education.

items.title: Charting the Trajectory of Artificial Intelligence Agents in Air Traffic Control
items.abstract: The aim of the study was to chart the evolution and the current research landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) agents within the domain of air traffic control. Using bibliometric analysis, the study identified major research trends and gaps and provided a consolidated reference for researchers. The analysis included 58 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The findings showed that the earliest publication in the dataset appeared in 1998 and that research output increased noticeably after 2022. Publication output peaked in 2025, with 16 articles, indicating growing scholarly interest in AI agents for air traffic control. Citation analysis identified Agogino and Tumer’s (2012) article as the most influential publication, with 68 citations. The article introduced a multi-agent approach to air traffic flow management. Brittain and Wei’s (2022) article ranked second, with 54 citations, highlighting the increasing role of reinforcement learning. At the country level, the United States had the highest total citation count, followed by China, France, England, and Spain. By examining AI agents as a distinct research topic, the study provides a focused overview of an underexplored area relevant to researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

items.title: Epistemic Hidden Defects in Artificial Intelligence: Classical ʿIlal al-Ḥadīth as a Framework for AI Verification
items.abstract: This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.

items.title: Game-Based Learning Experience and Occupational Health and Safety Learning Achievement: The Mediating Role of Learning Engagement in Vocational Training
items.abstract: Occupational health and safety is a mandatory component of public vocational training; however, lecture-based instruction may not sufficiently engage adult learners. This study examined the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement, with learning engagement as a mediating variable, among occupational health and safety trainees at the South Jakarta Regional Job Training Center, Indonesia. A quantitative explanatory survey was conducted with all 174 participants enrolled in the 2026 Batch 1 regular and Mobile Training Unit classes using saturated sampling. All participants completed a game-based learning session on the Wayground platform, formerly known as Quizizz. Data were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire adapted from established instruments and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The game-based learning experience had a positive and significant effect on learning engagement (β = 0.854, p < 0.001) and learning achievement (β = 0.592, p < 0.001), while learning engagement had a positive and significant effect on learning achievement (β = 0.343, p = 0.016). Learning engagement partially mediated the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement (indirect effect = 0.293, p = 0.017). The model explained 72.9% of the variance in learning engagement and 81.6% of the variance in learning achievement. Approximately one-fifth of participants reported technical barriers, primarily unstable internet connections, system lag, device limitations, and game time limits perceived as too short. The findings suggest that game-based learning activities can enhance learner engagement and perceived learning achievement in occupational health and safety training for adult vocational learners, provided that adequate technical readiness is ensured.

items.title: Governance Framework and Overall Readiness for AI Enabling in Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Digital transformation in Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh’s RMG and SME sectors has become very popular because of the need for transparency and digital compliance by foreign customers as well as demand forecasting, inventory control, logistics, traceability and operational decision-making. But most organizations could not implement Artificial Intelligence and digital technology yet. The research reviews several academic papers, industry surveys, institutional reports, government sources and other secondary sources to investigate how prepared Bangladesh is to enable, use and maintain digital technologies like Artificial Intelligence in its supply chain management and what the challenges are there. Studies suggest that high cost of implementation, insufficient number of experts, weak digital infrastructure and the unreadiness of employees and supply chain partners to adapt to a new system are the very obstacles in implementing AI not just in Supply Chain Management but also in various other departments of an organization. Other than that, big firms like export-oriented firms tend to be more prepared than SMEs in accepting advanced digital systems due to a financial and technological edge. To understand this unevenness, this research proposes a ‘Two-axis Digital Readiness Matrix’ which is based on an organization’s internal capability and digital connectivity with external supply-chain partners. This study recommends higher opportunities for financing, advancement of workforce skills, increase in management capability and digital integration among supply chain participants

items.title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
items.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can realistically review and annotate, making labeled data a major bottleneck for developing supervised learning approaches. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as weak annotators in other domains, their effectiveness for cybersecurity tweet classification and downstream training of domain-specific pre-trained language models (PLMs) remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose a Teacher-Student weak supervision framework in which a selected LLM serves as a Teacher to generate weak labels for unlabeled cybersecurity tweets, enabling the training of cybersecurity-specific PLMs without large-scale manual annotation. Experimental results show that PLMs trained solely on LLM-generated labels consistently achieve F1 scores above 0.92, remaining within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across all evaluated architectures. These findings suggest that LLM-based weak annotation offers a practical alternative for constructing cybersecurity-specific training data when expert annotation resources are limited.

items.title: Operation Dark Clark: AI‑Enabled Russian Disinformation in Latin America and the Campaign to Shape Brazilian Politics (2020–2026)
items.abstract: This thesis reconstructs and critically evaluates Operation Dark Clark, a Russia-origin influence operation that OpenAI reportedly disrupted and publicly documented on 8 October 2026. It assesses the operation as the first influence campaign ever classified by the company in Category 5 of the IO Breakout Scale—its highest rating for a disrupted operation—and the most complex false-front identity it had dismantled in two and a half years of systematic reporting. The operation combined generative artificial intelligence with classical intelligence tradecraft. It recruited unwitting employees in Latin America to staff a seemingly legitimate organization called the “Social Research Center” (SRC), which was controlled through a fabricated persona named “Mia Clark.” Her published corpus comprised more than sixty original research articles examining public opinion on BRICS and comparing the Brazilian economy under Presidents Jair Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Drawing on an open-source intelligence (OSINT) verification protocol that distinguishes documented and verified facts from attributed claims and editorial speculation, the thesis traces the operation’s activities across Argentina, Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Panama, and Brazil. It reconstructs the operation’s institutional lineage, from Soviet active measures through the Internet Research Agency, PeaceData (2020), and the Prigozhin-linked “Politology”/“La Compañia” network, reportedly now under the control of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). The study situates the case within the broader industrialization of AI-enabled information confrontation, examining the contemporaneous Iranian “Bogus Bylines” operation and the transnational Pravda network. A dedicated chapter investigates the October 2026 Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers and the observed 94% collapse in automated traffic across the Yandex network, cautioning against unwarranted causal interpretations of the relationship between these events. The thesis argues that Dark Clark represents a doctrinal evolution from platform-based amplification toward institutional laundering: the introduction of synthetic or co-opted authority into established media organizations and academic institutions. It contends that effective democratic resilience requires a multilayered response combining platform transparency, institutional source verification, provenance standards, and robust fact-checking capacity. The analysis deliberately refrains from endorsing the unverified assertion circulating in Brazilian political commentary that the operation materially influenced Brazilian electoral outcomes.

items.title: Principles of Good Scientific Practice in Geoinformatics: From Data Management to Reproducible Code
items.abstract: Principles of Good Scientific Practice in Geoinformatics: From Data Management to Reproducible Code Trial lecture (Probevorlesung, § 13 HabilO) for the Venia Legendi in Geovisual Analytics at the Faculty of Environmental Sciences, Technische Universität Dresden (October 15, 2026, Dresden, Germany). Reflecting the core principles discussed, this lecture and its underlying pipeline are openly archived as a version-controlled, persistent resource to demonstrate reproducible scientific practice in action. Abstract Spatial data science occupies a uniquely vulnerable position in the ongoing reproducibility crisis. Below high-level Python libraries lies a complex stack of compiled C/C++ system libraries (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ) where unannounced datum shifts or compiler updates silently alter coordinates without throwing errors. Concurrently, spatial planning practice frequently relies on GUI-based desktop GIS workflows and binary office documents (`.docx`), leaving zero audit trail for legal scrutiny or scientific verification. Grounded in the normative framework of the DFG Code of Conduct (Guidelines 7, 10, 11, and 12) and Mayer's principles of multimedia learning, this lecture outlines four foundational pillars to transition from fragile ad-hoc scripts to resilient, verifiable scholarship: Part I • Diagnose (The Reality Check): Identifying the root failure modes of spatial data science—from the "spatial curse" of compiled system dependencies and unrecorded point-and-click operations to the administrative friction of managing 22,000+ data cells across municipal Word documents. Part II • Structure (The Resilient Archive): Establishing core architectural principles: Separation of Concerns (SoC), Single Source of Truth (SSOT), and Knowledge Longevity. Demonstrating that tools (Typora, QGIS, Zotero) are merely disposable viewing lenses, whereas disciplined plain text (Markdown) and open formats (GeoPackage, GeoParquet) constitute the permanent archive of thought. Addressing the FAIR vs. ELSA dilemma through synthetic twins and probabilistic hashing. Part III • Construct (Freezing the Computation): Demonstrating parameterized, headless GIS batch pipelines. Using an authentic planning case study (1,500 wind turbine viewsheds calculated via headless GRASS GIS inside JupyterLab for regional planning), the lecture illustrates literate provenance, isolated Docker container layering (Carto-Lab), and automated GitLab CI/CD release pipelines. Part IV • Evaluate (The Generative Frontier): Governing the integration of non-deterministic Large Language Models (LLMs). Establishing Prompts as Code and conversational lineage archiving to maintain human-in-the-loop accountability, separating probabilistic model outputs from verifiable scientific scholarship. The lecture concludes with a pragmatic survival checklist for Master's theses and frames Good Scientific Practice through the lens of Calm Technology: disciplined conventions do not add administrative burden - they liberate researchers from technical friction to focus on intellectual synthesis. items.title: Sci$Π$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

items.title: The AI Mirror: A Qualitative Study of Student Autonomy and Dependence in ESL Writing
items.abstract: This article explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in English as a Second Language (ESL) writing, examining whether it fosters autonomy or promotes dependency. Utilizing a qualitative methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted following a timed writing task with 40 intermediate-level ESL students across three higher education institutions in Oman. Thematic analysis reveals that AI's impact on student autonomy is highly contingent upon its pedagogical application. When utilized strategically for brainstorming and personalized feedback, AI acts as a scaffolding tool that fosters self-directed learning. Conversely, when students rely on AI to generate complete texts or passively correct errors, they experience cognitive offloading, leading to decreased independence. The study emphasizes the need for educators to cultivate digital literacy, promoting an approach that empowers students to use AI as an intellectual partner rather than a cognitive replacement.

items.title: The Utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technology in Islamic Religious Education to Develop Students’ Spiritual Character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Gedong Tataan District, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and its contribution to strengthening students’ spiritual character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province. The study was motivated by the challenges of providing relevant and engaging Islamic Religious Education for a digitally oriented generation, whose familiarity with technology is not always accompanied by strong spiritual awareness. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. The informants included the Head of the Madrasah, IRE teachers, students, dormitory Ummi, and PMDL administrators. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observations, and documentation of IRE learning activities. The findings indicate that AI was utilized through several applications, including AI-based chatbots to facilitate students’ religious inquiries and spiritual guidance, interactive digital applications to support dhikr and self-reflection (muhasabah), and visual-based AI learning platforms to present Islamic Religious Education materials in a more engaging manner. These applications supported interactive religious learning, encouraged students to reflect on their behavior and religious practices, increased learning motivation, and strengthened emotional engagement with Islamic learning. However, the findings also demonstrate that AI has a supportive rather than substitutive role in spiritual character formation. Teachers remain essential in modeling and cultivating values such as sincerity, patience, discipline, and closeness to Allah SWT through direct guidance and interpersonal interaction. The novelty of this study lies in identifying AI as a complementary pedagogical instrument that connects digital Islamic learning with students’ spiritual self-reflection, while emphasizing the irreplaceable role of teachers in authentic spiritual character formation. This study contributes to the development of technology-integrated Islamic Religious Education by proposing a balanced approach in which AI supports learning innovation without displacing teacher-mediated spiritual formation.

items.title: WORK ENVIRONMENT, WORK SUPERVISION, JOB TRAINING, AND OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY FOR CONSTRUCTION WORK PRODUCTIVITY
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of work environment, work supervision, and job training on occupational safety and health (K3) and work productivity, as well as the effect of K3 on work productivity among 200 employees at CV Griya Fajar Konstruksi, South Tangerang. A quantitative approach was employed using survey data from 200 employees and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that work environment and work supervision have positive and statistically significant effects on K3 and work productivity, while K3 has the strongest positive relationship with work productivity (β = 0.989; p < 0.001). In contrast, job training shows negative and statistically significant relationships with K3 (β = −0.437; p = 0.034) and work productivity (β = −0.285; p = 0.041). Five of the seven hypotheses are supported. The findings qualify the expected positive role of training by indicating that its provision alone does not necessarily translate into improved safety and productivity. The findings also highlight the importance of integrating supportive working conditions, consistent supervision, effective K3 practices, and relevant and practical training to support safe and productive construction operations.

items.title: XARA: A Multimodal Agentic System for eXtended Reality Experiment Generation
items.abstract: Controlled experiments are essential for advancing transportation research, yet designing eXtended Reality (XR) environments for behavioural studies remains technically demanding and inaccessible to many domain researchers. Current workflows require proficiency in game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, imposing significant barriers to rapid scenario prototyping and iterative experiment design. This paper presents XARA, a novel system that integrates a dual large language model (LLM) architecture with an immersive XR environment to enable voice driven experiment generation for transportation research. XARA employs a pipeline in which spoken natural language commands are first transcribed and then interpreted into structured commands that manipulate a Unity based XR scene in real time. The system supports object creation, spatial manipulation, animation control, and scene persistence through a modular architecture. By lowering the technical threshold for XR experiment creation, XARA enables transportation researchers to rapidly prototype driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios using intuitive voice commands and hand gestures within an immersive 3D environment. This paper describes the system architecture, the voice to command pipeline, and discusses potential applications across behavioural travel experiments, safety studies, human factors research, and policy testing.

items.title: “It Felt Like Practicing Telemedicine While Learning About It”: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Medical Students’ Reflective Diaries from a Telemedicine Elective Course Across two Cohorts
items.abstract: Abstract Background Telemedicine has shifted from a niche modality to an established component of routine clinical practice in many health systems. Medical curricula are only beginning to address this shift. Reflective writing is increasingly used both as a pedagogical tool in medical education and as a data source for qualitative research on student attitudes. The experiences and conceptual journeys of pre-clinical medical students enrolled in dedicated telemedicine instruction are under-studied, particularly across multiple cohorts spanning the COVID-19 and post-pandemic periods. Methods We conducted a reflexive thematic analysis of 81 reflective diaries written by students (predominantly second-year medical students) enrolled in an elective telemedicine course at a single Israeli medical school across two cohorts distinguished by consent procedure: a retrospective cohort (2019–2024, n = 39), in which students who had already submitted diaries as a routine course component were contacted by email in 2025 (after ethical approval was granted) and asked to consent retrospectively to use of their diaries in research; and a prospective cohort (2025, n = 42), in which students were informed at the start of the course that the diaries would be analyzed and were asked to enclose a signed consent form with the diary they submitted. Analysis followed Braun and Clarke’s six-phase reflexive thematic analytic framework with an inductive orientation. Results Six overarching themes were identified: (1) a transformative conceptual journey from skepticism or naïveté to conviction; (2) telemedicine as the inevitable trajectory of medicine and a site of professional-identity formation; (3) recognition of telemedicine as a holistic discipline drawing on multiple lenses; (4) a productive tension between equity gains and erosion of the doctor–patient bond; (5) lived experience (as patient, family member, or in prior professional roles) functioning as an explicit interpretive lens; and (6) pedagogy and the medium of delivery, with the Zoom format read by students as enacting the course’s argument. The thematic structure was stable across cohorts. Distributional shifts in the prospective (2025) cohort included articulation of artificial-intelligence displacement concerns, focused engagement with breaking-bad-news as a boundary case, named concerns about defensive prescribing, the war (October 2023 onward) as a catalyzing event alongside COVID-19, increased advocacy for converting the course from an elective to a curricular requirement, and emerging attention to online patient and clinician communities as a distinct dimension of digital medicine. Conclusions This multi-cohort qualitative analysis identifies six stable themes and documents strong, consistent positive engagement with a pre-clinical telemedicine elective across both cohorts. Students describe the course as a formative and highly valuable learning experience, engage substantively with the multi-dimensional character of telemedicine, and read the Zoom delivery format as enacting the course’s content — an effect we describe as pedagogical resonance. Differences in the articulation of certain sub-themes (notably AI-displacement concerns and humanistic boundary cases such as breaking bad news) were more prominent in the prospective (2025) cohort and reflect the evolving discourse on digital medicine; these are cross-sectional differences and do not warrant longitudinal or causal inference. Taken together, our findings make a strong case for the inclusion of dedicated telemedicine instruction as a core component of the pre-clinical medical curriculum.

items.title: “NEW HUMANISM” AS A FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE IN THE WORKS WRITTEN BY K. ISHIGURO AND Y. TAWADA
items.abstract: The article conceptualizes the artistic dimensions of “new humanism” in transcultural prose, based on K. Ishiguro’s novels “Never Let Me Go”, “Klara and the Sun” and Y. Tawada’s “Suspicious Characters on a Night Train”. It is suggested that rapid technological progress, the emergence of artificial intelligence, and the crisis of traditional humanistic values manifested in the studied works require a re-evaluation of the human essence in the era of metamodernism. The sense of alienation and the inability to become a part of any community make it possible to examine the literary works through the lens of the postcolonial theories. Thus, the article also analyzes the transition from postmodern irony to metamodernist “new sincerity” under the conditions of technological progress. The poetics of representing this new identity and the transformation of the “self-other” dichotomy are investigated through the material of contemporary British and Japanese literature. It is established that despite the challenges of digitalization, basic ethical guidelines remain the foundation of humanistic values in any era, particularly in times of severe social challenges. Universal categories such as empathy, love, kindness, tolerance, respect for biological differences, and the ability to bear responsibility for one’s own inventions and actions acquire particular significance. As a result of the study, it has been proven that the writers gradually abandon postmodern irony and nihilism, turning to the so-called “cautious optimism”. It has been substantiated that K. Ishiguro and Y. Tawada overcome cultural dislocation by creating a special third, intermediate space where a world-open personality is formed.

items.title: “Time and Position”, Cosmic Principle, and Delights in Heaven: Examining the View of Shengsi 生死 (Life and Death) in the Study of Yijing
items.abstract: The problem of shengsi 生死 (life and death) is one of the most fundamental and intractable questions of human existence, yet remarkably little systematic work has been done on the Yijing’s own conception of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) as an integrated philosophical and religious problem. Drawing on the Yijing text, the later commentaries, and conceptual analysis, this study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the Yijing’s conception of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) in its three basic structural perspectives: “time and position” (shi wei 時位), the cosmological alternation of yin and yang, and the existential posture of “delighting in Heaven” (le tian 樂天). The first perspective shows that sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) are situational states depending on one’s circumstance within changing configurations of time and position. The second perspective lifts this situational awareness to the level of cosmic principle: sheng 生 (life) being the union of yin and yang, si 死 (death) as their separation, both of which are necessary phases in the endless process of cosmic generation. The third perspective traces the process by which this cosmological understanding was internalized. It leads to an existential attitude of “delights in Heaven and knows his own fate and what Heaven bestows” (le tian zhi ming 樂天知命), a condition in which the fear of si 死 (death) is overcome by acceptance. In this case, the meaning of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) is fulfilled in the realization and accomplishment of one’s “will” (zhi 志) and “nature” (xing 性) endowed by Heaven. The study concludes that the Yijing offers a philosophical and religious vision in which sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) are not opposed and separated, but integrated as complementary phases of a single, ongoing process of cosmic and human realization. It speaks to the perennial human question of how finite beings, conscious of their mortality, can find meaning and fulfilment in a world of constant change.

items.title: 3D Digital Modeling Empowering Sculpture Education
items.abstract: This paper explores the application of 3D modeling software in sculpture education and proposes a data-driven framework called “Adaptive Sculpture-3D,” aimed at addressing the lack of real-time feedback and the challenges of cognitive load management in traditional teaching. Through case analysis and quantitative experiments, the study validates the effectiveness of the framework in improving students' creation accuracy (with a 21.8% reduction in vertex error rate) and self-efficacy (medium effect size of 0.74), while also revealing limitations in enhancing operational efficiency (effect size of 0.38). The experimental results demonstrate that the real-time feedback mechanism of the framework significantly optimizes the learning process, though caution is needed to avoid learner dependency caused by excessive prompts. This research provides empirical support for the digital curriculum design in art institutions and envisions future developments integrating generative artificial intelligence and multimodal data.

items.title: 44th National Congress of the Italian Society of Nephrology Nurses (SIAN)
items.abstract: The 44th National Congress of the Italian Society of Nephrology Nurses (SIAN), held in Bologna, Italy, from 4 to 6 May 2026, provided a national forum for discussion on the evolving role of nursing in nephrology. The Congress was preceded by a dedicated pre-congress session focused on education, research, and clinical practice, with particular attention to the involvement of nursing students and early-career professionals in scientific activities. Across plenary sessions, round tables, workshops, oral communications, and digital poster presentations, the scientific programme addressed major areas of contemporary nephrology nursing, including professional development, patient-centred care, vascular access management, dialysis technologies, kidney transplantation, symptom management, home and community care, digital health, artificial intelligence, sustainability, and nutritional care. Particular attention was given to the integration of evidence-based practice, clinical expertise, technological innovation, interprofessional collaboration, and patient education. This Conference Proceedings provides an overview of the scientific and educational activities of the meeting and brings together the accepted contributions presented during both the pre-congress session and the main Congress. Collectively, these contributions illustrate the diversity and continued development of nephrology nursing practice and research in Italy and highlight the importance of scientific societies in promoting professional competence, knowledge exchange, and innovation in kidney care.

items.title: A de-identified inpatient clinical pathway dataset integrating ICD-10 diagnoses, ICD-9-CM procedures, Indonesian Case-Based Groups (INA-CBG), and length of stay for healthcare analytics
items.abstract: Background Healthcare administrative databases have become indispensable resources for healthcare analytics, hospital management, clinical pathway analysis, health services research and artificial intelligence. Modern hospital information systems routinely collect standardized diagnoses, procedures, reimbursement classifications, and hospitalization outcomes in everyday clinical practice. Despite their importance, publicly accessible datasets integrating diagnosis codes, procedure codes, case-mix classifications, and hospitalization outcomes remain scarce, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The absence of comprehensive administrative datasets limits reproducible research in clinical pathway modelling, healthcare operations, reimbursement analysis, and machine learning. To address this gap, we developed and publicly released a de-identified inpatient clinical pathway dataset derived from routine hospital administrative records processed through the Indonesian Case-Based Groups (INA-CBG) reimbursement system. Methods The dataset was constructed from finalized inpatient hospitalization records collected between November 2016 and April 2026. Clinical diagnoses were represented using the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10), and clinical procedures were encoded using the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM). Each hospitalization episode included one primary diagnosis, up to 11 secondary diagnoses, one primary procedure, up to 16 secondary procedures, one INA-CBG classification code, one INA-CBG description, and one length-of-stay (LOS) variable. Data extraction, transformation, harmonization, de-identification, quality assessment, and validation were performed using a reproducible Python-based computational workflow. The final repository contained 165,391 hospitalization episodes represented by 32 standardized variables. Conclusions The dataset provides an openly available resource for healthcare analytics, clinical pathway research, process mining, hospital management, reimbursement analysis, predictive modelling, explainable artificial intelligence, and healthcare operational research. The combination of standardized ICD-10 diagnoses, ICD-9-CM procedures, INA-CBG classifications, and hospitalization outcomes enables diverse secondary analyses while maintaining interoperability with existing healthcare information systems. All datasets, metadata, source codes, and supporting documentation are publicly available through Zenodo to facilitate transparency, reproducibility, and future methodological development.

items.title: A digital leadership cycle for strengthening primary teachers’ lesson planning
items.abstract: Background—Primary teachers need support to translate digital access into pedagogically coherent lesson plans and teaching materials. Objectives—This study examined five connected aspects of principals’ support: diagnosing digital-learning needs, enabling situated professional learning, orchestrating digital resources, evaluating practice and renewing support, and synthesizing a cross-case leadership cycle. Method—A qualitative multiple-case study was conducted in four public primary schools in Muaro Jambi, Indonesia. Four principals and eight experienced upper-primary teachers participated, providing accounts complemented by non-participant observations and school documents. Within-case summaries and cross-case matrices were interpreted through source and method triangulation and member checking. Results—The cases shared needs diagnosis, workplace learning, resource coordination, and formative supervision, but differed in the evidence used, learning arrangements, and access constraints. Teaching materials considered in the study included teaching modules, worksheets, digital media, and assessments; no standardized improvement scores were available. Education-report analysis was prominent in Case A and Case B, peer-supported learning in Case C, and phase-based discussion in Case D. The synthesis yielded a diagnose–enable–evaluate–renew cycle, with resource orchestration embedded in enablement. Conclusions—The cycle offers a context-sensitive explanation of leadership support for digital lesson planning. It is an interpretive proposition for further testing, rather than evidence of causal effects on teacher competence or student outcomes.
